'''Zachary D. Blount''' is an American evolutionary biologist best known for his work on the evolution of a key innovation, aerobic growth on citrate, in one of the twelve populations of the [[E. coli long-term evolution experiment|''E. coli'' long-term evolution experiment]].  Blount is an assistant professor and Director of Graduate Education Innovation in the Department of Microbiology, Genetics, and Immunology at [[Michigan State University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Zack Blount |url=https://mgi.natsci.msu.edu/people/micro-biographies/dr-zack-blount.aspx |access-date=2025-11-08 |website=mgi.natsci.msu.edu |language=en}}</ref> He was previously a postdoctoral research assistant for [[Richard Lenski]] and a visiting assistant professor of biology at [[Kenyon College]] from 2018 to 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kenyon.edu/directories/campus-directory/biography/zachary-blount/|title=Zachary D. Blount|website=www.kenyon.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-08-03|archive-date=2018-08-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180803074618/https://www.kenyon.edu/directories/campus-directory/biography/zachary-blount/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.blount-lab.org|title=Blount Lab|website=Blount Lab|language=en|access-date=2018-08-03}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Zachary D. Blount was born and raised in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] where he developed an early interest in [[science]]. He earned high honors in Biology at [[Georgia Institute of Technology]], where he was introduced to microbiology by [[professor emeritus]] [[Thomas Tornabene]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.blount-lab.org/about-me.html|title=About Me|website=Blount Lab|access-date=2016-03-05}}</ref> He obtained his [[Master's degree|master's]] from the [[University of Cincinnati]], where he worked on insertion sequence elements of [[Extremophile|hyperthermoacidophilic]] [[Archaea]] of the genus ''[[Sulfolobus]]'' under the guidance of Dennis Grogan. He moved to Michigan State University in 2003 for his [[Doctorate|doctoral]] work with Richard Lenski.

== Research ==
In 2003, 15 years and 33,000 generations after Richard Lenski had set up the [[E. coli long-term evolution experiment|long term evolution experiment]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/evolving-e-coli|title=Evolving E. coli|website=Science News|date=13 December 2012 |access-date=2016-03-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lenski|first=Richard E.|date=2011-01-01|title=Evolution in Action: a 50,000-Generation Salute to Charles Darwin|journal=Microbe Magazine|volume=6|issue=1|pages=30–33|doi=10.1128/microbe.6.30.1|doi-access=}}</ref> one lineage of ''[[E.coli]]'' began to show very high [[turbidity]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn14094-bacteria-make-major-evolutionary-shift-in-the-lab#.UlIWqCRJOAg|title=Bacteria make major evolutionary shift in the lab|last=Holmes|first=Bob|website=New Scientist|language=en-US|access-date=2016-03-13}}</ref> Work done by postdoctoral researcher Christina Borland showed that this elevated turbidity was due not to [[contamination]], and confirmed that aerobic growth on citrate had spontaneously evolved in the population.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nxtbook.com/nxteu/BBC/knowledge_200904/index.php?startid=42#/48|title=BBC Knowledge - April 2009 - Evolution in Action|website=www.nxtbook.com|access-date=2016-03-05|archive-date=2016-03-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160318014403/http://www.nxtbook.com/nxteu/BBC/knowledge_200904/index.php?startid=42#/48|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Blount went on to conduct a series of "evolutionary replay experiments" in which he replayed the evolution of the population in which aerobic citrate usage evolved from different clonal [[genotype]]s isolated from different time points to examine how the propensity to mutate to Cit<sup>+</sup> changed. This analysis involved examination of several trillion [[bacteria]]l [[Cell (biology)|cells]], and showed that clones from later generations had significantly increased rates of mutation to Cit<sup>+</sup>, indicating that evolution of the trait in the population was contingent upon a history in which "potentiating" mutations accumulated that made it mutationally accessible. Later genomic analysis of clones from the population established the immediate [[Genetics|genetic]] and [[Biochemistry|biochemical]] basis of the Cit<sup>+</sup> trait to be a tandem duplication mutation that placed a silent citrate transporter gene under the control of a new promoter that caused its expression when oxygen is present, an example of promoter capture and gene [[exaptation]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/evolutionary-innovation-caught-in-the-act/2012/09/19/d9698b6e-0296-11e2-9b24-ff730c7f6312_story.html|title=Evolutionary innovation caught in the act|last=Boytchev|first=Hristio|date=2012-09-19|newspaper=The Washington Post|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286|access-date=2016-03-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn14094-bacteria-make-major-evolutionary-shift-in-the-lab#.UlIWqCRJOAg|title=Bacteria make major evolutionary shift in the lab|last=Holmes|first=Bob|website=New Scientist|language=en-US|access-date=2016-03-05}}</ref> Based on these findings, Blount proposed a model for the evolution of [[complex traits]]: 1. potentiation, in which mutations that make the trait evolutionarily accessible accumulate, 2. actualization, in which a mutation produces a phenotypic switch in which the new trait is manifested, and 3. refinement, in which natural selection accumulates subsequent mutations that make the new trait more effective.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_videos.jsp?cntn_id=125492&media_id=73143|title=News - Video - Postdoc researcher Zachary Blount discusses discovering the process of ''E. coli'' evolution. {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=2016-03-05|archive-date=2017-05-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517174045/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_videos.jsp?cntn_id=125492&media_id=73143|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Currently, Blount is further investigating how complex traits evolve, how novel traits impact ecology, and how [[speciation]] occurs in [[Asexual reproduction|asexual]] populations based on models proposed by Fredrick Cohan of [[Wesleyan University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ncse.com/book/export/html/2593|title=Bacterial speciation|website=ncse.com|access-date=2016-03-05}}</ref>
